title: When the Letters Sings
premise: Dominic Okafor, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who writes novels by night, has spent five years in the safe harbor of her coastal town after a betrayal in her twenties that she has never named. When a snowstorm strands her former best friend and rival novelist, Ada Reyes, at the lighthouse during the town's winter festival, the two are forced to confront the man they both loved and the manuscript they wrote together and tore apart. As the festival approaches, Dominic must decide whether reclaiming her voice means forgiving Ada — and the version of herself who chose ambition over honesty. The book ends with the festival's closing night, where Dominic reads the finished novel aloud, Ada at her side, both finally at peace with the people in the mirror.
about_author: Jonah Yarrow is the pen name of a former lighthouse keeper's assistant who traded fog signals for fiction and now writes from a drafty cottage on the northern coast. When the Letters Sings is a debut novel drawn from a decade of watching storms roll in and people wait them out.

chapters.title: The Light Keeps Its Own Hours
chapters.summary: Dominic Okafor's POV. Five years into her quiet life tending the lighthouse ledger and writing unpublished chapters, Dominic catalogs her safe routines. When the harbormaster warns of an early snowstorm, she battens down alone, relieved. Emotional beat: the comfort of smallness, and the faint ache of what safety has cost her.

chapters.title: What the Storm Brings In
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The storm hits harder than forecast, and a car slides to a stop at the lighthouse gate: Ada Reyes, her former co-author and rival, half-frozen and furious to be rescued. Dominic takes her in with brittle courtesy. Emotional beat: shock and resentment crackling under forced hospitality.

chapters.title: Two Beds, One Truth
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ada and Dominic circle each other through the first night, trading barbed politeness about their split five years ago — a manuscript, a man named Elias, and a betrayal neither will name. Emotional beat: the past pressing in through every careful silence.

chapters.title: The Manuscript in the Drawer
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Searching for a blanket, Ada finds Dominic's drawer of unfinished pages — including pages in Ada's own handwriting, kept all these years. She says nothing, but it rearranges her. Emotional beat: the discovery that she was kept, not discarded.

chapters.title: Snowbound Rules
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Roads closed, phone lines down; the festival committee's messages stop mid-sentence. The two women negotiate a truce of chores and hours, and Dominic admits, obliquely, that she never stopped writing. Emotional beat: grudging respect taking root in shared labor.

chapters.title: Elias, Briefly
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A radio bulletin mentions Elias Marsh — now a celebrated novelist — winning a prize for a book that reads, unmistakably, like theirs. Ada confesses she suspected for years. Emotional beat: the old wound reopened, and the relief of finally showing it.

chapters.title: What Each of Us Did
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The first true fight: Dominic accuses Ada of selling the manuscript to Elias; Ada reveals Dominic signed away the rights herself, in grief, and forgot. Both retreat. Emotional beat: the shattering of a five-year story each woman told herself.

chapters.title: The Festival Below
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Through binoculars they watch the town string festival lights in the snow, small and stubborn against the dark. Dominic admits she has refused invitations for five years. Ada admits why she really came north. Emotional beat: tenderness arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Chapters We Never Wrote
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada proposes finishing the old manuscript together, as an act of reclamation, not profit. Dominic refuses — finishing it means admitting what she lost. Emotional beat: hope offered and flinched from.

chapters.title: The Person in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Alone at dawn, Dominic reads her old rejection letters and the contract she signed, and finally sees her own hand in the ruin — not just Ada's, not just Elias's. Emotional beat: the brutal, freeing turn toward self-honesty.

chapters.title: Thaw Lines
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A partial thaw lets a supply truck through with festival mail — including a letter from Elias to Dominic, asking to meet. Ada reads it first and must choose whether to hand it over. Emotional beat: loyalty tested by old jealousy.

chapters.title: The Letter Sings
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic reads Elias's letter: he wants to adapt 'their' book and asks her blessing, believing she was the wronged one. Instead of triumph she feels complicity. Emotional beat: the realization that forgiveness is not a verdict but a practice.

chapters.title: Confessions by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada confesses her own worst act — she let Elias believe Dominic abandoned the book, because she wanted him, and wanted the story. Dominic listens without absolution. Emotional beat: the raw cost of telling the whole truth.

chapters.title: A Door Left Open
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic doesn't forgive — not yet — but she leaves Ada's door unlocked, and sets two places at breakfast. They work in silence, side by side, on separate pages. Emotional beat: forgiveness beginning as a gesture, not a feeling.

chapters.title: The Road Clears, the Choice Doesn't
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The roads open; Ada could leave for the city and her own deadline. Instead she unpacks the car. Dominic, offered a meeting with Elias, drafts a reply and deletes it three times. Emotional beat: the terrifying freedom of choices no longer forced by circumstance.

chapters.title: Rival Lines
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Old competitive habits flare when a festival organizer invites both women to read at the closing night — same stage, same slot. They almost sabotage each other, then catch themselves laughing. Emotional beat: rivalry transmuted into partnership.

chapters.title: Elias Comes North
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Elias arrives unannounced, charming and entitled, expecting gratitude. Dominic tells him the book was never only his, and refuses the adaptation — but also refuses to perform victimhood. Emotional beat: reclaiming the narrative without cruelty.

chapters.title: The Last Draft
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. With two days to the festival, Ada and Dominic write through the night, finishing the manuscript they abandoned five years ago — arguing, laughing, weeping. Emotional beat: creation as reconciliation; the past rewritten by finishing it.

chapters.title: What the Mirror Says Now
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The night before the reading, Dominic forgives herself — aloud, in the lighthouse mirror, the sentence she has avoided for five years. Emotional beat: quiet, earned self-forgiveness as the story's hinge.

chapters.title: The Closing Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the festival's final night, Ada and Dominic read the finished novel aloud, alternating chapters, before a town that has watched them circle each other for a week. Emotional beat: public vulnerability; the light finally turned outward.

chapters.title: After the Applause
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Elias slips out early; Ada lets him go without a scene, discovering she no longer needs his verdict. She and Dominic walk the seawall, talking about the next book — two books, actually, and one they might write together. Emotional beat: the future opening without guarantees.

chapters.title: The Light Keeps Turning
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Epilogue in spring: the manuscript is with an editor, Ada's room above the lighthouse is now permanent, and Dominic logs the light each evening as always — but the ledger now holds two names. Emotional beat: peace as a practice, not an ending.
